newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine sugar producers meet to save industry.
newsitem.headline: Philippine sugar producers meet to save industry.

text.p: Philippine sugar millers and planters were meeting with government officials on Friday to plead for measures to help the industry after the country's biggest miller reported a debt problem, officials said.
The planters and millers were in talks with officials of the Sugar Regulatory Administration (SRA) at the Malacanang presidential palace, an SRA official told Reuters.

Asked if the Victorias Milling case would be discussed, he said: "I don't know. Regional committees formed earlier to draft proposals on how to revitalise the Philippine sugar industry will present their recommendations today to the Presidential task force."
On Thursday, sugar miller Victorias Milling met with creditor banks to negotiate a moratorium on principal repayments on its debts amounting to 4.4 billion pesos.
The loans were taken from 32 banks.
Earlier this year, President Fidel Ramos formed a committee to map out measures to save the sugar industry.

Last month, Philippine sugar millers and farmers asked the government to suspend the 35 percent tariff rebate on refined sugar imports from neighbouring countries to protect the local industry. Under present rules, the Philippines gives a 35 percent tariff discount on refined sugar imports from member-nations of the Association of Southeast Asian nations.

Sugar planters and millers have said the over importation of some 1.2 million tonnes of sugar, mostly refined sugar from neighbouring ASEAN countries, between September 1995 and July 1996 pushed the prices of raw sugar to as low as 500 pesos per 50-kilogram bag last year from 750 to 800 pesos at the start of 1996.
To prop up local sugar prices, the government has authorised state-owned National Food Authority to buy up to 200,000 tonnes of domestic sugar at 610 pesos per 50-kg bag.

Agriculture Secretary Salvador Escudero has also asked the Tariff Commission to raise duties on imported sugar to 133 percent from 100 percent from January 1 to June 30, 1997 and, to 100 percent from 80 percent from July 1 to August 31. Industry officials said Victorias Milling's financial problems had strengthened their case that the industry needed protection.
